prompt: A rider's height on a Ferris wheel is $h(t) = 20 - 18\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{15} t\right)$ meters, $t$ seconds after boarding at the bottom. How fast is the rider rising at $t = 7.5$ seconds? Round to two decimal places (meters per second).
hint: The rising speed is $h'(t)$. The $20$ vanishes; $-18\cos(\text{inside})$ needs the chain rule with inside $\frac{\pi}{15}t$.

hints.text: The rising speed is $h'(t)$. The $20$ vanishes; $-18\cos(\text{inside})$ needs the chain rule with inside $\frac{\pi}{15}t$.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: $\frac{d}{dt}\left[-\cos(2t)\right] = -(-\sin(2t)) \cdot 2 = 2\sin(2t)$. Two minus signs cancel and the inside rate comes along. Same thing here with $18$ and $\frac{\pi}{15}$.

explanation: Chain rule on $-18\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{15}t\right)$: the outside gives $+18\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{15}t\right)$ (two minus signs cancel), and the inside derivative is $\frac{\pi}{15}$.

At $t = 7.5$: $\frac{\pi}{15} \cdot 7.5 = \frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1$, so $h'(7.5) = \frac{6\pi}{5} \approx 3.77$ m/s. That is the rider's fastest climb, exactly level with the hub at height $20$ m.

alternativeExplanations.title: Check with circular motion
steps: The wheel has radius $18$ m (the amplitude) and period $\frac{2\pi}{\pi/15} = 30$ s, so the rim moves at $\frac{2\pi \cdot 18}{30} = \frac{6\pi}{5} \approx 3.77$ m/s.
At $t = 7.5$ s, a quarter turn in, the rider is level with the center and moving straight up, so all of that rim speed is vertical.
At the top or bottom the vertical speed is $0$ (the sine factor is $0$), and $h'(t)$ reaches its maximum $3.77$ m/s only at the sides, confirming the formula.
